title: Decoding AI — What the promise of artificial intelligence means for developing economies
gist: Drawing on the World Development Report 2026, Lall and Nayyar argue AI's biggest opportunity in developing economies is extending scarce expertise (not replacing surplus workers), but warn below-cost AI pricing is an introductory offer that could lock low-bargaining-power countries into a few providers. They prescribe 'adopt, adapt, then advance', cost-conscious procurement with anti-lock-in clauses, and investment in complements (power, connectivity, literacy).

insights.claim: The advanced-economy framing of AI as a threat to white-collar jobs misses its biggest opportunity: in much of the developing world the binding problem is too few skilled workers, not too many.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Reframes the EM AI demand case around labor-scarce expert services (health, agronomy, public services).
insights.quote: In much of the developing world, the problem is too few skilled workers, not too many
insights.locator: Most of what we hear about

insights.claim: AI has reached lower-income countries 40 times faster than the internet did.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Unusually fast diffusion suggests EM user bases for AI services can scale rapidly.
insights.quote: AI, which has reached lower-income countries 40 times faster than the internet did, can extend scarce expertise to far more people in far less time.
insights.locator: Most of what we hear about

insights.claim: Lower-income countries have fewer than 20 radiologists per million people, roughly a fifth of an adequate level, a gap AI is beginning to close.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Large addressable gap for AI diagnostic imaging in low-income markets.
insights.quote: Lower-income countries have fewer than 20 radiologists per million people, roughly a fifth of what is considered adequate

insights.claim: AI-assisted screening in Bangladesh raised daily diabetic retinopathy screenings by 40 percent; AI weather forecasts in India reached 30+ million farmers; Ghana's Rori SMS math tutor delivered a year of learning gains at US$5 per student.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Low-cost, basic-phone-delivered AI shows strong unit economics in EM health, ag and edtech.
insights.quote: In Ghana, the Rori math tutor, delivered by text message on basic phones, produced a year of learning gains at US$5 per student.

insights.claim: A few companies in a few economies control the most advanced AI models, the chips and the data centers, letting developing economies customize world-class AI cheaply but on others' terms.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Market concentration in frontier AI is an explicit policy concern for multilateral lenders.
insights.quote: A few companies in a few economies control the most advanced AI models, the chips they depend on, and the data centers that run them.

insights.claim: Many AI providers price access below cost to drive adoption, gather data and embed themselves, mirroring ride-hailing platforms that raised prices once they became the default; today's low AI prices may be an introductory offer.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Implies future AI pricing power for incumbents and margin expansion once switching costs set in; also regulatory backlash risk.
insights.quote: Today's low prices with AI products may likewise be an introductory offer.

insights.claim: Once AI adoption crosses a threshold and switching becomes costly, developing economies with limited bargaining power and thin competition-policy capacity are most exposed to dependence on a few providers.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Expect EM governments to push data portability, exit clauses and open-weight alternatives in AI procurement.

insights.claim: Locally built language models such as India's Sarvam AI and Africa's InkubaLM, plus open-weight models, give countries alternatives, which in a concentrated market are the foundation of bargaining power.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Tailwind for open-weight and local-language model developers as sovereign hedges.
insights.quote: in a concentrated market, alternatives are the foundation of bargaining power
insights.locator: Adapting AI is also a path

insights.claim: Hyperscalers' capital expenditure is projected to exceed US$750 billion in 2026, more than the GDP of many countries, which makes pushing the AI frontier unaffordable for most developing economies.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Data point on 2026 AI capex scale; reinforces that EMs will be AI consumers, not frontier builders.
insights.quote: hyperscalers' capital expenditure is projected to exceed US$750 billion in 2026, more than the GDP of many countries

insights.claim: AI's expected productivity impact in advanced economies is twice that in developing economies, and three-quarters of that gap reflects differences in adoption.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: AI likely widens the AE-EM productivity gap unless adoption barriers fall.
insights.quote: Its expected productivity impact in advanced economies is twice that in developing economies, and three-quarters of that gap reflects differences in adoption.

insights.claim: In Sub-Saharan Africa nearly a third of rural schools lack reliable electricity, more than two-thirds lack dependable internet, and nearly nine in ten 10-year-olds cannot read a simple text.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Infrastructure and foundational-skill deficits cap near-term AI monetization in SSA.
insights.quote: nearly nine in ten 10-year-olds cannot read a simple text

insights.claim: Almost half of internet-derived training data is in English while more than 2,000 languages are spoken in Africa alone, so local-language data is both a necessity and a bargaining asset.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Local-language data becomes a strategic asset; opportunity for data-collection and localization players.
insights.quote: Local-language data is both a necessity and an asset to bargain with.

insights.claim: Countries with little capacity to detect malicious AI uses are more vulnerable to AI-enabled cyberattacks.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Cybersecurity demand rises alongside AI adoption in low-capacity states.

insights.claim: Off-the-shelf AI is not enough: a clinical decision-support tool trained in high-income countries can recommend what does not fit local medical norms, so adaptation drives adoption.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Localization layer is where value accrues for EM AI deployments.
insights.quote: Adaptation grounds AI in local realities, which drives adoption.
insights.locator: Pushing the AI frontier is enormously expensive

insights.claim: Only 17 of nearly 10,000 published studies on AI in health care show causal evidence of impact in low-resource settings, and 80 percent of digital agencies in lower-income countries have no or only basic ways to evaluate AI tools.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Evidence gap means EM public AI demand will favor proven back-office predictive tools over novel applications.
insights.quote: Only 17 of nearly 10,000 published studies on AI in health care show causal evidence of impact in low-resource settings

insights.claim: The most immediate government AI opportunity lies in proven back-office predictive analytics and decision support, and governments in lower-income countries overwhelmingly rely on predictive rather than generative AI.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Near-term EM public-sector AI spend skews to predictive analytics vendors.

insights.claim: Governments should procure AI with price protections, data portability, exit clauses and interoperable systems, and plan for costs after introductory prices end.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Procurement terms that compress vendor lock-in and future pricing power in public-sector AI deals.
insights.quote: Procurement should guard against lock-in through price protections, data portability, exit clauses, and interoperable systems.

insights.claim: Regulators should start with voluntary testing standards and existing data-protection, consumer-safety and cybersecurity rules, then build competition authorities that understand AI markets before concentration hardens into dependence.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Signals likely direction of EM AI regulation: light-touch initially, competition-focused later.
insights.quote: build competition authorities that understand AI markets — before concentration hardens into dependence
